summary: The note follows the lifecycle of electronic devices from mining and manufacturing through consumer use to disposal and recycling, framing e-waste as a growing global and local problem. It describes Greenfield City's e-waste program, recycling and urban mining, circular economy design, education efforts, extended producer responsibility legislation, and economic incentives. It stresses that collective action by innovators, policymakers and communities is needed.
one_line: Overview of the electronic device lifecycle and e-waste challenge, covering recycling, urban mining, circular economy, local programs, legislation and economic incentives.
key_facts: The International Waste Management Symposium reported on September 5th, 2023 that the world generates about 50 million tons of e-waste every year, and only 20% is formally recycled.
Unrecycled e-waste often ends up in landfills, where toxic substances leach and pose environmental and health risks.
MacroChip Inc., which processes silicon into chips, launched its new sustainability program on October 21, 2023.
Emily Nguyen, a local electronics store manager, observed on November 12, 2023 that smartphone lifecycles have shortened significantly over the past decade.
City Recycling Coordinator Michael Clark said on December 1, 2023: "E-waste is not just a local issue, it's a time bomb for our planet."
Greenfield City initiated a pioneering e-waste management program on January 15, 2024, spearheaded by Mayor Linda Kim.
A special e-waste collection event was held on February 28th as part of the Greenfield City effort.
At a March 10, 2024 open house, EcoCycle Innovations CEO Jonathan Price demonstrated shredding and sorting of e-waste into core materials for reentry into manufacturing.

Dr. Hannah Rodriguez of the Institute of Sustainable Resources said on April 2, 2024 that reclaiming one gram of gold from electronics requires roughly 5% of the energy needed to mine it from the earth.
Dr. Oliver Bennett led a May 3, 2024 workshop on enhancing the circular economy through design for recycling: fewer toxic materials, modular designs for easy repair, and standardized components.
School principal Jessica Edwards launched an e-waste education initiative in local schools beginning June 2023.
Senator Christopher Yu introduced legislation on July 4, 2024 establishing extended producer responsibility (EPR) laws to hold manufacturers accountable for end-of-life product management.
The Financial Summit for Sustainable Electronics, slated for August 28, 2024, will discuss tax breaks, recycling subsidies and penalties for improper disposal.
